subject: Cooking
title: Why Onions Make You Cry
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Why Onions Make You Cry.

hook.text: You slice an onion and within seconds, tears stream down your face. It's chemical warfare.

buildup.text: Cutting ruptures onion cells, releasing enzymes that convert sulfur compounds into a volatile gas.

discovery.text: That gas — syn-propanethial-S-oxide — reacts with moisture in your eyes to form sulfuric acid.

twist.text: Chilling onions slows the enzyme reaction, producing less gas and fewer tears.

climax.text: Japanese scientists bred 'tearless' onions by silencing the gene for the lachrymatory enzyme.

punchline.text: Onions evolved tear gas as a defense. We eat them anyway.

quiz.question: What does chilling an onion before cutting do?

details.summary: Cutting an onion breaks cells that release an enzyme which converts sulfur compounds into syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a volatile gas that irritates the eyes. The cornea's nerve endings trigger tears as a protective reflex. Chilling onions slows the enzymatic reaction and reduces gas production.
details.whyItMatters: Onion chemistry demonstrates how enzymes and substrates interact when cell walls break. This same principle applies to garlic's pungency and mustard's heat when crushed.
takeaways: Cell damage releases enzymes that create a tear-inducing gas
Chilling onions slows the enzymatic reaction significantly
Sharp knives crush fewer cells, reducing gas release

faq.question: What is the best way to avoid crying while cutting onions?
faq.answer: Chill onions for 30 minutes to slow enzyme activity. Use a very sharp knife to crush fewer cells. Cut near a vent or fan to disperse the gas. Cutting under running water works but is impractical. Some people wear goggles for heavy onion prep.

faq.question: Do all onion varieties make you cry equally?
faq.answer: No. Sweet onions like Vidalias have less pyruvate, the precursor to the tear gas compound, so they produce fewer irritants. Red and white onions vary. Scallions and leeks produce much less. Breeders have developed reduced-tear onion varieties.
